contentBlocks.body: A for loop in Python works on any iterable. It calls iter() on the object to get an iterator, then calls next() on the iterator until it raises StopIteration. This is the same protocol as JavaScript's Symbol.iterator and next(), with StopIteration taking the place of { done: true }.

contentBlocks.code:
nums = [10, 20]
it = iter(nums)
print(next(it))   # 10
print(next(it))   # 20
next(it)          # raises StopIteration -- a for loop catches this for you

contentBlocks.body: A function that contains yield is a generator function. Calling it runs none of its body; it returns a generator object. Each next() resumes the body until the next yield, hands out that value, and pauses again with all local variables intact. Generators are lazy: they produce values only when asked, so they can describe huge or even infinite sequences.

contentBlocks.code:
def countdown(n):
    print("start")
    while n > 0:
        yield n
        n -= 1
    print("done")

gen = countdown(2)     # prints nothing yet
print(next(gen))       # start, then 2
print(next(gen))       # 1
print(list(gen))       # done, then []

contentBlocks.body: A generator expression is a comprehension in parentheses. It produces items lazily instead of building a list, which matters when you only need to aggregate or stop early.
A generator can be consumed only once. After list(gen) has drained it, a second list(gen) returns []. Call the generator function again to start over.
yield from other_iterable yields every item of another iterable in turn, like yield* in JavaScript.

payload.explanation: Calling a generator function only creates the generator; the body starts running at the first next().

knowledgeItems.prompt: gen = (x * 2 for x in [1, 2]); what does print(list(gen), list(gen)) show?

payload.explanation: The first list() exhausts the generator, so the second one gets no items.

knowledgeItems.prompt: What exception signals that an iterator has no more items?

payload.explanation: next() raises StopIteration when the iterator is exhausted; for loops catch it and end quietly.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Why write sum(x * x for x in data) instead of sum([x * x for x in data])?

choices: it avoids building the whole intermediate list in memory
it runs the loop in parallel
payload.answer: it avoids building the whole intermediate list in memory
payload.explanation: The generator expression produces one value at a time for sum to consume.
